title: Effects of Paraxanthine and Alpha-GPC, Alone and Combined, on Exercise Performance, Metabolism, and Cognition in Resistance-Trained Adults
official: Effects of 7-Day Paraxanthine, Alpha-GPC, and Combined Supplementation on Resistance Exercise Performance, Resting Energy Expenditure, and Cognitive Function in Resistance-Trained Adults: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Crossover Trial
summary:
The goal of this clinical trial is to learn whether taking paraxanthine, alpha-GPC, or both together for 7 days improves resistance exercise performance and mental performance in healthy, resistance-trained adults aged 18 to 40. Paraxanthine is the main compound the body produces when it breaks down caffeine. Alpha-GPC is a source of choline, a nutrient the body uses to make a chemical messenger involved in attention and muscle contraction. The study will also look at resting metabolism and safety.

The main questions it aims to answer are:

* Does paraxanthine, alpha-GPC, or the combination increase the number of repetitions and the total amount lifted on the bench press and leg press?
* Does paraxanthine, alpha-GPC, or the combination improve attention and reaction time?
* Does taking both together work better than taking either one alone? Researchers will compare each supplement condition with a placebo (a look-alike capsule with no active ingredient) to see if the supplements change exercise performance, mental performance, and resting metabolism.

Participants will:

* Complete a first visit for health screening, a body composition scan, and maximal strength testing on the bench press and leg press
* Take capsules once a day for 7 days in each of 4 conditions (placebo, paraxanthine, alpha-GPC, and both combined), in random order, with 7 days off between conditions
* Not know which capsules they are taking, and the researchers testing them will not know either
* At the end of each 7-day period, visit the lab after an overnight fast for resting metabolism measurements before and after taking the capsules, a small blood draw (about 4 teaspoons), computer-based attention and reaction-time tests, and bench press and leg press sets to failure
* Avoid caffeine, alcohol, and hard exercise before testing visits, and keep a daily log of sleep and any side effects
criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

* Age 18 to 40 years
* Resistance-trained for at least 6 months
* Familiar with the bench press and leg press or squat movement patterns
* Healthy and non-smoking
* Habitual caffeine intake of 300 mg/day or less
* Willing to abstain from caffeine, energy drinks, nicotine, alcohol, vigorous exercise, and non-essential dietary supplements before testing sessions
* Able to complete a 10 to 12 hour overnight fast before testing visits

Exclusion Criteria:

* \- Pregnant or breastfeeding
* Cardiovascular, renal, hepatic, metabolic, neurologic, or psychiatric disorders
* Resting blood pressure of 140/90 mmHg or higher at screening, confirmed on repeat measurement
* Arrhythmia or physician-advised restriction from exercise
* Diagnosed sleep disorder or current shift work
* Current use of psychoactive medications, stimulants, beta-blockers, cholinergic or anticholinergic agents, monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs), selective serotonin or serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs/SNRIs), or supplements that affect exercise performance, heart rate, blood pressure, sleep, or cognition
* Allergy or intolerance to methylxanthines, paraxanthine, alpha-GPC, choline-containing products, maltodextrin, or capsule ingredients
* Recent musculoskeletal injury that limits exercise testing
* Gastrointestinal disorders that affect supplement tolerance or absorption

sites.f: Exercise Physiology and Nutrition Laboratory (EPNL) at Jacksonville State University
